title: Preaching, Baptism and Worldly Wisdom
english: […] “us may be one” (John 17:21–22).

“Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you?” (1 Corinthians 1:13). If someone else endured the cross for us, let us be called his. If perhaps we were baptized into someone else’s name, let him have us, and let us enroll him as Savior and Redeemer. But if “Christ died for our sins” (1 Corinthians 15:3), and with him alone we have been “buried through baptism into death” (Romans 6:4), then let him, he says, possess those who have been bought. For we have been saved through him and by him, who laid down his own life for us (1 John 3:16).

“For Christ did not send me to baptize, but to preach the gospel” (1 Corinthians 1:17). He was admittedly sent to proclaim Jesus to the Gentiles. But we say that it also belongs to the work of an apostle to baptize some, as the occasion and need require, if he so chooses. So that he would not seem to spend the time owed to preaching on other pursuits, he very rightly left this to be done at leisure by those in each region and by all who were appointed to oversight. He himself preached the gospel instead, since he had been entrusted with the ministry of the word and had searched out the mystery of Christ with great precision. Yet just as the inspired Stephen, though appointed a servant of tables, did not set aside the duty of teaching the mysteries (Acts 6:2–5), so too the inspired Paul, though appointed to preach the mystery of Christ, also met the need for baptism when the time came. Authority for both lay before him, and nothing prevented him from doing it if he chose.

“Where is the wise man? Where is the scribe? Where is the debater of this age?” (1 Corinthians 1:20). To those who pride themselves on worldly wisdom and do not accept the faith, clearly meaning faith in Christ, the gospel is foolishness. But it is not so with us; far from it. For we are convinced that it is the power of God (1 Corinthians 1:18), a way of salvation that leads to sanctification, and that by its abundant preaching it wisely guides us to the knowledge of the truth.

I for my part think that here he calls the orators “wise,” who by the cleverness of their speeches always wove persuasion into falsehood and strove to win for it the appearance of truth. By “scribes” I think he means the schoolmasters or grammarians, whose custom it was to labor over the writings of the poets and to explain them to the young. By “debaters” he means those who are used to fighting over words and who, supposedly with precision, put things to the test. Through the concepts they devise they pretend to seek the truth, that is, whatever seems, as far as possible, to stand beyond reproach on each question set before them. But they do not do it rightly at all; rather, they do it with utter carelessness. For they have not known the God of all, who without toil framed this whole universe by ineffable workings, and by a mere nod brought into being all things that were not. So the wisdom of the world has truly been made foolish (1 Corinthians 1:20).

“For since, in the wisdom of God, the world did not know God through wisdom, it pleased God through the foolishness of the preaching to save those who believe” (1 Corinthians 1:21). He calls even human understanding and eloquence, that is, the very bloom of style, “the wisdom of God,” to teach that God is the maker of the mind and the giver of good sense and eloquence, even if some have used them for ends they should not. By “the foolishness of the preaching” he means the plainness of the words. For the inspired disciples were unskilled in speech but rich in knowledge (2 Corinthians 11:6).

“For Jews ask for a sign, and Greeks seek wisdom” (1 Corinthians 1:22). Paul’s statement is true on both counts. Once, when Christ was driving out of the temple courts those who sold sheep and oxen, turtledoves and pigeons, and saying, “Do not make my Father’s house a house of trade” (John 2:14–16), they retorted, “What sign do you show us, since you do these things?” (John 2:18), and, “Who gave you this authority?” (Matthew 21:23). Some of the scribes also came to him, after a very great display of signs, and said with malice, “Teacher, we wish […]” (Matthew 12:38).

title: God’s Weakness Is Stronger than Men
english: […] “to see a sign from you” (Matthew 12:38). So, counting the words of the saints as worth almost nothing, words through which they could well have learned that he was the Christ, they kept demanding signs from God. That is why the Savior said to those sent by John, “Go and tell John what you hear and see: the blind receive their sight, the lame walk,” and so on (Matthew 11:4–5).

The Greeks, for their part, seek brilliance of diction and argument, and they think even the way of the dispensation in the flesh to be foolishness. They say, “Why was it necessary at all for the Word who is from God, being God by nature and able to accomplish whatever he purposes by will and nod, to become man and to endure death? How could a virgin give birth?” they say. “And how will what death has destroyed rise again?” But it is not at all surprising that they say such things: “For the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit, for they are foolishness to him” (1 Corinthians 2:14).

But to us it is the power and wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24). For through him God the Father has saved the whole world under heaven, as through the power that is naturally his and through his own ineffable wisdom. For the Son is the wisdom and power of God the Father, through whom all things were brought into being and, once made, are preserved.

And if anyone, he says, should choose to measure the power that is in God against the powers of men, he will certainly see that whatever among the divine works may seem to have been done as in weakness, and as it were not with the full power of its Maker, is beyond and better than all human strength. You will understand wisdom in exactly the same way: what seems to be foolish is wiser than men. Suppose someone wished to compare the small and least of created things with the size and beauty of the elements, I mean heaven and the sun and the other stars, and fire and water and the rest. The power and wisdom found in the small things would be very slight, and, judged by their inferiority at least, it might seem a [lacuna] sort of thing. Yet no one among us could become the maker even of things so [lacuna]. Truly, then, “the weakness of God is stronger than men, and the foolishness of God is wiser than men” (1 Corinthians 1:25). So the dispensation holds all wisdom, for Christ has reigned with understanding, in wisdom, over the whole world under heaven.

“Proclaiming to you the testimony of God” (1 Corinthians 2:1). He calls Christ the testimony of God, for God the Father bore witness to him, saying, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17).

“And I was with you in weakness and in fear,” and so on (1 Corinthians 2:3). Although I used such modest instruction, he says, I was very much afraid that my words, if they proved too lofty for the understanding you had, would do you no good but rather harm. For those who are infants in mind, a tender and gentle word would suit their learning, “but solid food is for the mature, for those who by practice have their senses trained to distinguish good and evil” (Hebrews 5:14). So my word to you, he says, came as in great weakness, and not with the full power of one who teaches the mysteries. Nor was it “in persuasive words of human wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power, so that your faith might not rest in the wisdom of men but in the power of God” (1 Corinthians 2:4–5).

For to their preaching the apostles added signs from God as well. They made the deed itself a clear demonstration that one must believe that God was attested in them, through the Spirit and through the deeds themselves, since they used a certain ineffable and inexpressible power and working and performed their wonders with ease. The little myths of the Greeks would naturally need an eloquence to fight in their defense and, as it were, to cover up their ugliness. But for the divine preaching a plain and gentle word suffices, attested as it is by the power of God.

θεοσημίαι rendered 'signs from God' (divine signs, wonders).

In 'through the power that is naturally his and through his own ineffable wisdom' (τῆς ἐνούσης αὐτῷ φυσικῶς ... τῆς ἑαυτοῦ), both pronouns refer to the Father, the subject of the clause; the next clause names the Son as the Father's wisdom and power, which is Cyril's point.

In 'if they proved too lofty for the understanding you had' (ἀμείνους τῆς ἐνούσης ἡμῖν εὑρισκόμενοι διανοίας), the plural subject is taken as Paul's words, and ἡμῖν ('in us') is read as ὑμῖν ('in you'), a common itacism; the sense requires the Corinthians' understanding.
'Christ has reigned with understanding' (βεβασίλευκε συνετῶς) may echo Psalm 47:7–8 (LXX 46:8–9, ψάλατε συνετῶς· ἐβασίλευσεν ὁ θεός); possible allusion only, not cited inline.
'God was attested in them, through the Spirit and through the deeds' may recall Hebrews 2:4; possible allusion only.

title: Wisdom Hidden from the Rulers
english: “Yet a wisdom not of this age, nor of the rulers of this age, who are coming to nothing” (1 Corinthians 2:6). The word of the holy teachers of the mysteries goes forth in lowly speech, yet it plants in us an unadulterated knowledge of the divine mysteries. It shows that Christ is wisdom, not through the fine speech of the world’s wise men, but as he is attested by his own nature. None of the rulers of this age knew him (1 Corinthians 2:8). These rulers are the evil and hostile powers, who have spoken through the wise men of the world.

“For if they had known, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2:8). The saying is very reasonable. For by his own cross Christ triumphed over the evil and hostile powers, nailing to the wood “the bond written against us” (Colossians 2:14–15). He drove Satan away from his tyranny over us, abolished the sin of the world, opened the gates of Hades to the spirits below, and pulled down the power of death. How, then, could the suffering on the cross be anything but hateful to the unclean demons? So they would not have crucified him, had they known for certain that he was the Redeemer and the Lord of glory.

That the crucifixion of Christ, carried out through the madness of the Jews, was the work of the devil’s savagery, the inspired John showed plainly when he said of Judas, “After the morsel, Satan entered into him” (John 13:27). Satan did not know that Jesus was God. For if he had known and been convinced of it, how could he have tempted him in the desert, saying, “If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become loaves of bread” (Matthew 4:3)? And the Savior himself, as all agree, took care to escape the notice of the rulers of this age, so that, unnoticed, he might suffer, and by his own blood win for himself and for his own Father all that lies under heaven.

“Even the depths of God” (1 Corinthians 2:10). The depths of God are the hidden knowledge laid up in the sacred writings. The Spirit knows it and reveals it to the souls of the saints, and makes the mind within them a divine mind.

“The natural man” (1 Corinthians 2:14). The natural man is the one who lives according to the flesh and has not yet had his mind enlightened through the Spirit. He has only the inborn, human understanding which the Creator puts into the souls of all.

“But the spiritual man judges all things” (1 Corinthians 2:15). The spiritual man judges all things and, so to speak, sifts them finely with exact care, but he himself is judged by no one. That those called natural need spiritual teachers, by all means, for their benefit and training, Paul makes plain by adding, “For who has known the mind of the Lord, so as to instruct him?” (1 Corinthians 2:16; Isaiah 40:13). It is as if he said: No one could instruct the natural man unless he had the mind of Christ. By “instruct” he means “prepare him to understand.” And who are those that have the mind of the Lord? He showed this himself when he went on, “But we have the mind of Christ” (1 Corinthians 2:16), that is, the Spirit who speaks in the saints, unveils mysteries to them, and makes the mind within them a divine mind.

So, although the saints could have understood and spoken things better and loftier than what they wrote, they wisely measured their teaching to the state of those they were leading into the mysteries.

“And I, brothers, could not speak to you as to spiritual men, but as to men of the flesh, as to infants in Christ” (1 Corinthians 3:1). It was not for want of a word strong enough to raise you to perfect knowledge that I was kept from speaking to you of the more perfect things. It was because you are infants in your condition and have an unsteady mind, one that has not yet advanced to the knowledge of the more perfect things and cannot yet take in mysteries.

“I planted” (1 Corinthians 3:6). Paul planted, Apollos watered, and God called them to growth. What, then, is the planting, if not what belongs to the beginning of faith: to acknowledge and to say that God is the Lord of all? And what is the watering, if not the sowing and pouring in, as it were, of the words that come from teaching, which nourish the believer’s mind to strength so that it may also prove fruitful?

The last sentence runs across the section break: the source puts its final words 'πιστεύσαντος νοῦν ἵνα φαίνοιτο καὶ καρποφόρος;' at the head of the next section. They are translated here so the question is whole; the next section begins with the following question ('τίς δὲ ἡ αὔξησις...').
Lemma lines from 1 Corinthians (bold in the print) are given in quotation marks with their reference; Cyril's comment follows each.
ψυχικός is rendered 'natural' (the traditional rendering), following Cyril's own definition: one who lives by the flesh with only inborn human understanding.
μυσταγωγοί / μυσταγωγούμενοι rendered 'teachers of the mysteries' / 'those they were leading into the mysteries'.
'τὸ καθ' ἡμῶν χειρόγραφον' (Colossians 2:14) rendered 'the bond written against us'; 'τεθριάμβευκε ... τὰς δυνάμεις' echoes Colossians 2:15, so the citation covers 2:14–15.

'ἀνήκας' is read as 'opened' (from ἀνίημι, 'let open'); the form is irregular in the printed text. 'opened the gates of Hades to the spirits below' may echo 1 Peter 3:19 and 'pulled down the power of death' may echo Hebrews 2:14; both are possible allusions only and are not cited inline.
The tempter's words 'these stones … loaves' (οἱ λίθοι οὗτοι ἄρτοι) are Matthew's wording (Matthew 4:3); Luke 4:3 has a single stone.
1 Corinthians 2:16 quotes Isaiah 40:13 (LXX); both are cited.
'νοῦν ... δυναμένοις' (dative plural) is read as referring to the saints who wrote (as if δυνάμενοι); the sense is that they could have said more but measured their teaching to their hearers.
ἀνασφαλής rendered 'unsteady' (not secure), as the context requires.
'ἐκάλει πρὸς αὔξησιν Θεός' rendered 'God called them to growth'; 'them' is supplied for English.
